notes.meaning: John sees another angel come down from heaven with great authority. He shines so brightly that the whole earth is lit up, as if he has just come from God's presence. Older writers were not sure whether this is Christ himself or a mighty angel sent by him. Wesley adds that if a servant shines like this, the Lord must be far more glorious.

The angel shouts that Babylon has fallen. The words come from Isaiah 21:9, where the old city of Babylon fell, and saying them twice sounds like a funeral song. Here Babylon stands for a great, proud power that turned people away from God. Her ruin is so complete that only demons and unclean birds and beasts will live there, as people once said of empty ruins.

differ.view: Wesley read Babylon as Rome, and the chapter as a picture of the Roman church's fall.
Older Reformed writers like Barnes saw Babylon as the power of the papacy. Some modern Reformed teachers see the pagan Rome of John's own day.
Many see Babylon as an end-times world system or city ruled by the Antichrist, a final enemy of Christ. Some think the city will be rebuilt on the Euphrates River.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic writers say Babylon is pagan Rome or unfaithful Jerusalem, and cannot be the Catholic Church.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars read the chapter as a 'doom song' over the Rome of John's day, the city that was persecuting Christians.

notes.meaning: Now the reason for her fall is given. She led the nations into 'immorality', which here means spiritual unfaithfulness: leaving the true God for idols, like a wife leaving her husband. Kings joined her, and merchants grew rich from her love of luxury. She kept people tied to her by her wealth and pleasures.

A voice from heaven, likely God's or Christ's own, calls, 'Come out of her, My people.' God has people even inside Babylon, and he calls them out before judgment falls, as Lot was told to leave Sodom. If they stay, they will be pulled into her sins and share her punishment. The words echo the prophets' call to leave old Babylon (Jeremiah 51:6, 45).

differ.view: Barnes saw a call to leave the Roman church and said it justified the Reformation. Some modern Reformed teachers apply it first to Christians in John's day, who had to avoid the idol worship tied to Rome's trade.
Ellicott says this is not about physically leaving the city of Rome.
Many read it as a call to separate in heart and life from the world's sin and love of money and things.
Some say it speaks first to believers in a future time of great trouble, leaving a real city, and warn against leaders who misuse the verse to control people.

notes.meaning: Her sins are stacked up like a huge heap that reaches heaven. That picture means the very worst guilt. God had seemed to overlook them, but now he acts. When a people's sins reach up to heaven, God's anger reaches down to earth.

God orders that Babylon be paid back for what she did to others, especially to his people. 'Double' is a Hebrew way of saying full and complete payment. The cup she filled to harm others becomes the cup of her own punishment. Matthew Henry notes that private revenge is still wrong; this is God's judgment, carried out by those he appoints.

Her punishment will match her pride and her luxury. In her heart she boasts, 'I sit as queen,' sure that grief will never touch her. Ancient Babylon made the same boast in Isaiah 47. Pride like this is the spring that all her other sins flow from.

Because of her proud feeling of safety, her troubles come all at once, in 'one day', meaning suddenly. Death, grief and famine replace her feasting, and fire destroys her. The very things she felt safe from fall on her. All her strength cannot stand against the mighty Lord who judges her.

The kings who shared her sin and luxury weep as they watch her burn. Yet they stand far off, afraid of sharing her pain, and they cannot save her. They mourn the loss of their comforts, not their sin; Matthew Henry calls this 'worldly sorrow'. 'In a single hour' shows how suddenly it all ends.

The merchants weep too, because no one is left to buy their goods. The long list shows the riches pouring into the great city: gold, jewels, silk, rare woods, spices, food and animals. It ends with slaves, 'bodies and souls of men', meaning people bought and sold like cargo. Matthew Henry urges traders to seek the true riches of Christ, since earthly wealth can fly away.

differ.view: Wesley saw these goods as still used in Rome's worship, and said souls are 'bought and sold at Rome'.
Gill read the trade in souls as the selling of indulgences (paid pardons) and prayers for souls in purgatory.
Some note these are luxuries, not needs, and apply 'bodies and souls of men' today to human trafficking and pornography.

notes.meaning: The mourners now speak to the city directly. The ripe fruit she longed for, and all her fine food and bright clothing, are gone for good. Matthew Henry notes that God's church may fall for a time and rise again, but Babylon's fall is final.

The merchants who got rich from her stand far away in fear, weeping. They cry 'woe' over a city once dressed in fine linen, purple, gold and pearls. The city is pictured as a woman wearing the very goods they used to sell her.

The merchants end their cry: so much wealth, gone in an hour. Then ship captains and sailors join in, watching the smoke from far away. They throw dust on their heads, an old sign of deep grief. Much of this picture comes from Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, a great trading city that fell.

Heaven, God's people, the apostles and the prophets are told to rejoice. God has judged their case against the city that hurt them. This is not joy in anyone's pain, but joy that God's justice is shown. It is the opposite of 11:10, where the wicked cheered the death of God's witnesses.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic writers note that this city killed apostles, so it must be a city of the first century, such as pagan Rome.

notes.meaning: A mighty angel throws a huge millstone into the sea. It is a sign: Babylon will be thrown down with force and gone forever. Jeremiah used a similar sign for old Babylon, sinking a stone tied to his scroll in the river (Jeremiah 51:63-64). God's people can be sure this enemy will never trouble them again.

differ.view: Some say ancient Babylon was never destroyed like this, so the city must one day be rebuilt and then destroyed.

notes.meaning: All the sounds of a living city stop: music, workers' tools, the grinding of grain, a lamp in the window, the happy voices of a wedding. Rich and poor alike are gone, and no new families will fill the city again. Two reasons are given: her merchants grew proud as the world's great ones, and she fooled the nations with 'sorcery', meaning tricks and lies. The heavenly city is the opposite; it needs no lamp because God is its light (22:5).

differ.view: Gill took the 'sorcery' to mean false teaching and idol worship.
Some note the Greek word is linked to drugs, and see a kind of addiction to buying, fed by advertising.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic writers point out that these are scenes of ordinary city life, which do not fit Vatican City.

notes.meaning: Last, the blood of prophets, saints and all who were killed on earth is found in her. She not only fooled the nations; she killed those she could not fool. Jesus said something similar about Jerusalem (Matthew 23:35). Evil this great brings this great a ruin.

differ.view: Wesley said no city has clearer blood-guilt than Rome, first under the emperors and later in the killing of Protestants.
Some say only a worldwide system, not a single city, could be guilty of all this blood.
